work.title: The Father-thing
work.first_publication: The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction, December 1954

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: Eight-year-old Charles Walton is sent to fetch his father for dinner and comes back unable to say which of them to fetch: there are two, and they look alike. The one that comes in to eat is the father-thing. Charles finds his real father's remains stuffed in the garage trash barrel — dry, translucent, an emptied skin, the insides eaten and the place taken. He escapes out of his bedroom window and recruits Tony Peretti, a fourteen-year-old who has beaten up every boy in the neighbourhood and who responds to the story with immediate, matter-of-fact belief. Watching through the window, they see the father-thing go slack the moment Charles's mother leaves the room — it is operated from outside. They fetch Bobby Daniels, a nine-year-old who is 'the best' at finding, and he locates the controlling organism under a stone by the garage: a foot-long jointed bug. It escapes down its tunnel. The father-thing catches Charles and drags him toward the bamboo behind the garage, where a mother-thing is maturing in its cocoon, more larvae are newly laid, and a Charles-thing is already dark and ready. The father-thing begins tearing the cocoon open so the Charles-thing can feed on the boy — and then convulses and dies. Daniels has poured the drum of kerosene down the bug's tunnel. The three boys go looking in the driveway for the matches to burn the rest.

structure.form: continuous short story in five scenes, moving from dinner table to the ground behind the garage
movements: The dinner table: Charles cannot say which father to fetch; the reader sees the alien surface for an instant and it is gone.
The trash barrel: the discovery of the emptied skin, and the boy's flight over the roof.
Recruiting Peretti: the story told to a fourteen-year-old, and believed.
The window and the search: the father-thing goes slack; the controlling bug is found and gets away.
The bamboo: the nursery — mother-thing, larvae, and a Charles-thing already ripe — and the kerosene.
structure.point_of_view: third person, close to Charles, with two deliberate exceptions where the narration steps back to the parents' view. The story never explains the aliens beyond what three boys can work out by looking.
structure.note_on_scale: The horror escalates by inventory rather than by event: one father, then a mother in progress, then a row of larvae, then a copy of the boy himself. Nothing has to happen for the situation to get worse.

characters.name: Charles Walton
characters.note: Correctly perceives the substitution and is disbelieved and punished for saying so. His knowledge of the ground — 'nobody knew the way like he did' — is what keeps him alive.

characters.name: The father-thing
characters.note: Its menace is entirely parental. It never threatens; it disciplines. 'This is for your own good. I know best, Charles.' The horror runs on the ordinary authority of a father over a boy.

characters.name: June Walton
characters.note: Notices everything — the tension, the child's fear, that her husband is 'so strange' — and is steered away from acting on any of it. She is being farmed and does not know it.

characters.name: Ted Walton
characters.note: Present only as a discarded skin. The reader never meets him.

characters.name: Tony Peretti
characters.note: The story's structural surprise: he believes Charles at once, takes charge, arms himself, and is the one who shoots the thing in the eye. Competence arrives from the least likely quarter.

characters.name: Bobby Daniels
characters.note: Finds the controlling bug and, unprompted, solves the problem with kerosene — a method he attributes to his family's practice against mosquitoes in Virginia. He is the one who actually wins.

settings.name: The Walton house and dinner table
settings.note: The alien is first detectable at a meal, in the middle of ordinary domestic complaint about work and manners.

settings.name: The garage
settings.note: Where the substitution happened and where the remains are hidden. The father-thing repeatedly tries to get Charles back inside it.

settings.name: The bamboo and debris between garage and house
settings.note: The nursery. The story's real discovery: the household has been colonised from its own neglected ground, among rotting boards and garbage.

motifs: The emptied skin — survival of the outside with the inside eaten out
Discipline as threat: every menacing line the father-thing speaks is a thing a father might legitimately say
Children's competence against adult incomprehension; the adults are never told and never help
Being controlled from outside — the body goes slack the moment no one is watching
The domestic ground itself as the breeding site: the horror grows in the household's own uncleared rubbish
reading.significance: The premise is the one Jack Finney would publish as The Body Snatchers the following year, and the family resemblance is noted in the scholarship. What is Dick's own is the register: the substitute is frightening not because it is inhuman but because it is exactly as authoritative as a father is entitled to be, and the boy's testimony carries no weight against it. The story's engine is a child who is right and cannot be heard — the same structure as 'Roog', with the dog replaced by a son.
reading.textual_note: This story exists in at least three states. Dick sent Boucher and McComas a rewrite of eleven new pages with a new ending at their suggestion, and then, unprompted, a second alternative ending four pages shorter. Which ending stands in the published text, and what the discarded ones did, is a real editorial question this dossier cannot settle from the collected text alone.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a simulacrum indistinguishable from the person it replaced, operated from outside
the story turns on a criterion of the genuine that only a child can apply
the colonisation is domestic, and breeds in the household's own uncleared ground
the betrayer wears the face of the person most owed trust

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick gave a direct biographical origin for the story, and the letters document an unusually fussy revision history.

evidence.quote: I got the idea for "The Father Thing" from the fact that I was always afraid of my fat…
evidence.reading: An explicit statement of origin in fear of his own father. Rare directness from Dick about a story's source, and the sentence is cut off in the captured window — the full passage should be read before it is quoted.

evidence.source: Selected Letters — to Boucher and McComas, 2 September 1953
evidence.quote: Here is the rewrite on "The Father-Thing." Eleven new pages. A new ending, as you suggested
evidence.reading: The published ending was written at editorial request. The story as read is not the story first submitted.

evidence.source: Selected Letters — to Boucher and McComas
evidence.quote: here is another ending for "The Father-Thing." A shorter version: knocks off four pages.
evidence.reading: A third state, offered unprompted. At least three endings existed.

evidence.quote: I wrote "The Father Thing" years ago, back in the 'fifties, as I recall.
evidence.reading: Late-career recollection; he notes it has been reprinted repeatedly and that a class of students wrote to him about it.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.work: Philip K. Dick: Exhilaration and Terror of the Postmodern
evidence.quote: if [Dick] believes something more hopeful it is, as we shall see, neither a man nor a woman but a child
evidence.reading: Palmer places the story in an argument about where Dick locates hope. The reading is borne out by the text: every effective actor here is under fifteen.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: "The Father-Thing" hovers between metaphorical and literal
evidence.reading: Palmer also singles out the depiction of the boy as 'an ethically responsible person', and reads the story as mixing the fantastic with the ethically discursive.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.work: The Search for Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: "The Father-Thing" was a forerunner of Jack Finney's Invasion of…
evidence.reading: Priority claim over The Body Snatchers (1955). Worth checking against publication dates rather than accepted on assertion.

evidence.author: Anne R. Dick
evidence.work: The Search for Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: Did she think that Earl would be a father substitute for Phil and tell Phil this? ("The Father-Thing".)
evidence.reading: A biographical reading tying the story to a specific figure in Dick's childhood household. Anne Dick's proximity is both what makes this valuable and what makes it interested testimony.

contradictions.summary: Two different origins are offered for the same story.

claim_b.source: Anne R. Dick, The Search for Philip K. Dick
claim_b.text: Earl as a father substitute in the household

contradictions.note: Not mutually exclusive, and neither is disinterested: Dick is explaining himself to a correspondent, Anne Dick is reconstructing a marriage she was inside. Both kept.

open_questions: Three endings are documented in the letters. Which is in the collected text, and are the discarded pages extant in the Boucher correspondence or the manuscript record?

Anne Dick calls the story a forerunner of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. Finney's serial ran in Collier's from November 1954 and this story appeared in F&SF that December — the claim needs checking against exact dates before it is repeated.

The story is unusually specific about its three boys' ages, ethnicities and competences. Is there anything in the letters about the Daniels character, who solves the problem and is the only one given a family practice and a home state?
